title: You Have Your GCSE Results! But, Now What?
author: Dominic Salles
summary: On UK GCSE results day, English teacher Dominic Salles combines a personal narrative of his own disappointing 1980s O-level results with six concrete lessons for students navigating exam outcomes and the transition to A-levels. His first and most conceptual lesson names 'relative deprivation,' the tendency to judge results against classmates rather than the full national distribution, and uses his own recalculated statistics (a grade B that actually placed him in the national top 4.5-6 percent) to show how misleading peer comparison can be. The middle lessons cover adolescent brain development (the prefrontal cortex not maturing until 25, which he uses to counsel against harsh self-judgment), studying for enjoyment rather than market speculation, and a structured self-audit method for turning past revision habits into a improvement plan by writing down what was and wasn't done. His most evidence-dense sections address AI and spaced retrieval directly: citing studies that AI-assisted studying tends to produce worse outcomes because students offload thinking to it, he recommends using AI strictly as a testing tool rather than a teaching tool, and pairs this with an explicit Ebbinghaus forgetting-curve revision schedule (same day, then escalating intervals out to fourteen months) that he argues makes 20 minutes of daily distributed retrieval outperform 80-100 hours of April-to-exam cramming.
points: Salles operationalizes 'relative deprivation' with real numbers: a grade B he considered mediocre against his friends actually placed him in the national top 4.5-6 percent, once measured against the full cohort rather than a peer group of high-achieving classmates.

His AI guidance is specific and counter-intuitive: he cites research that AI-assisted study produces worse learning outcomes because students offload cognitive effort to it, but argues AI becomes highly effective when used exclusively as a retrieval-testing examiner rather than as an explainer.

The spaced-retrieval schedule he lays out (same day, next day, one week, two weeks, one month, two months, four months, six months, with a final test at fourteen months) operationalizes the Ebbinghaus forgetting curve into an actionable daily revision routine.

His time-cost comparison, 213 hours of twenty-minutes-daily spaced practice from the start of year 12 versus 80-100 hours of concentrated April cramming, reframes distributed practice as more total effort but far higher retention per hour, not simply as a shortcut.

His self-audit method (writing down exactly what revision was and wasn't done per subject, then comparing to results) turns results day into a diagnostic tool for the next exam cycle rather than a verdict, citing the act of writing the plan down as itself increasing follow-through.
quotes: So, lesson number one is not to compare yourself to your friends, compare yourself to the whole country. Only 20% of students in the country even get to a grade 7. Only 2.5% ever get a grade 9 in English.

You are a 16 year old, and your pre-frontal cortex isn't fully developed till you are 25. What that means is that, no matter how clever, or kind, or funny or enthusiastic you are, your brain is still not great at planning for the future.
Your exam results are a very, very good guide to how well you have revised, not how much, but how successfully.
Students who use AI to study are likely to do worse. It seems we tend to off load our thinking to AI. Even if AI teaches us really well, it seems we pay less attention to it than a real person.

But if I instead spent only 20 minutes a day, from the beginning of year 12, that's 213 hours. If, during those hours, I use the Ebbinghaus Forgetting Curve to decide on what to be tested on, I'll have an amazing memory of everything I've been taught.

That final test is not 6 months from now, it is 14 months from now. These gaps are big, which means after the first month you barely have to revisit stuff, but as long as you stick to these gaps, and test yourself, that memory is locked in.
Shit happens. It was all my own fault. Which was great, because that meant it was totally up to me to solve it. So I did.
